sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: This study aimed to determine pathologically how limb severity in chronic limb-threatening ischemia affects the great saphenous vein (GSV) wall, and whether it influences vein graft patency.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In 89 limbs undergoing infrainguinal bypass with the ipsilateral GSV, the intimal and medial thickness of the residual vein segment was measured. Wound (W), ischemia (I), and foot infection (fI) grades were assessed, with loss of primary graft patency as the endpoint.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Primary patency was 72.3% at 1 year and 59.3% at 2 years. Independent factors for patency loss were poor-quality vein (hazard ratio [HR] 3.12), severe W grade (HR 2.63), and cerebrovascular disease. Severe W cases had a thicker intima (56.0 vs. 28.1 μm, P <0.01) and media (310.4 vs. 255.8 μm, P = 0.02) than mild cases; the I and fI grades showed no differences. Between the patency-loss (n = 31) and maintained (n = 58) groups, intimal thickness was similar (51.2 vs. 44.1 μm, P = 0.57), whereas medial thickness differed (349.9 vs. 261.1 μm, P <0.01; area under the curve 0.65). Above versus below a 280-μm medial cutoff, patency was 43.0% versus 75.7% (P = 0.03).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Medial thickening of the preplacement GSV, seen with a severe wound grade, may be a critical factor in vein graft failure. (This is a secondary publication of Jpn J Phlebol 2025; 36: 89–97.)

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) is a condition in which atherosclerotic lower-extremity arterial disease produces limb ischemia. It not only has a profound impact on quality of life—including ambulation and wound healing—but also represents the most severe presentation of peripheral arterial disease, with the potential to result in major amputation.1) Limb severity in CLTI is an indispensable clinical parameter in treatment planning, serving both as a determinant of the revascularization strategy and as an independent predictor of wound healing.2)

The 2 principal revascularization options for CLTI are bypass surgery and endovascular therapy. In bypass surgery, an autologous vein is the conduit of choice, particularly for reconstruction of the below-knee arteries, and vein graft quality—defined by the use of the great saphenous vein (GSV) and by conduit diameter—correlates with postoperative patency.3,4) Although the patency of distal bypass using an autologous vein is favorable, no preventive strategy has yet been established for the graft stenosis that develops in 20%–30% of cases within 1–2 years after implantation.5) With respect to the effects of CLTI on the limb, an increase in inflammatory cells within the lower-limb skeletal muscle and an elevation of serum cytokines have been demonstrated, and CLTI has been reported to contribute to systemic inflammation originating from the limb.6) Because the GSV is the single most important conduit for surgical reconstruction in CLTI, and because CLTI exerts pro-inflammatory effects on the whole body, we focused on the morphological impact of limb severity on the GSV. The morphological effects on the preplacement GSV of the 3 components of the wound, ischemia, and foot infection (WIfI) classification—wound (W), ischemia (I), and foot infection (fI)—have not been adequately investigated. In the present study, we pathologically examined the influence of CLTI-related limb severity on the GSV wall in terms of wall thickness, and further analyzed whether such changes have any direct effect on vein graft patency.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: The present study analyzed 89 cases treated between 2010 and 2018 at Asahikawa Medical University Hospital, in which infrainguinal arterial bypass surgery was performed for CLTI using the GSV of the affected limb and the residual GSV segment was submitted for pathological examination. Because the aim was to analyze the influence of limb severity on the GSV, cases in which the GSV of the affected limb was not used for reconstruction, as well as cases in which a vein other than the GSV was submitted for pathological examination, were excluded from the analysis. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Asahikawa Medical University (approval number 22015).

sec.title: Collection of patient background and operative factors
sec.p: Clinical information was collected retrospectively from medical records. Operative variables comprised the GSV harvest site (thigh or crus and foot), vein graft quality, proximal anastomotic site, distal anastomotic site, and graft placement technique (single vein graft or spliced vein graft; in situ, reversed, or non-reversed translocation). Vein quality was defined with reference to the 1993 report of Sasajima et al.: a GSV with an internal diameter of 2.0–2.9 mm after intraoperative dilatation was classified as a poor-quality graft, whereas a diameter of >3.0 mm was regarded as a good-quality graft.7) Veins classified as good or fair were analyzed together as a single good-quality group and were compared with poor-quality veins. Limb severity was assessed according to the WIfI classification on the basis of preoperative or intraoperative findings. The I grade was evaluated by the ankle–brachial index or skin perfusion pressure. For fI, abscess formation or osteomyelitis demonstrated by magnetic resonance imaging or bone pathology was assigned grade 2, and bacteremia or sepsis was assigned grade 3. Based on the clinical findings, each factor was stratified into mild and severe categories as follows: W grade 0 or 1 was defined as mild and grade 2 or 3 (presence of necrotic findings) was defined as severe; fI grade 0 or 1 was defined as mild and grade 2 or 3 (presence of deep infection) was defined as severe.

sec.title: GSV pathological specimens and measurement of wall thickness
sec.p: Residual segments were obtained from the GSV of the affected limb. Using the in situ technique, the most distal portion of the harvested segment was used; when the vein was harvested from the thigh, as in the non-reversed or reversed techniques, the distal portion of the GSV was submitted for pathological examination. Between vein harvest and completion of the operation—an interval of approximately 2–3 hours—specimens were preserved in heparinized blood or normal saline. Immediately after the operation, they were fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin within 2 days. Because the GSV lumen was not pressurized during formalin fixation, the luminal dimensions of individual specimens could not be maintained at a constant size. Paraffin sections were cut at 5 μm. Wall thickness was measured on sections stained with elastica–Masson trichrome or elastica van Gieson staining, which permits the visualization of collagen and elastic fibers, including the internal and external elastic laminae. Each GSV cross-section was divided into 8 segments, and the intimal and medial thicknesses were measured using the open-source software ImageJ (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA; https://imagej.net/ij/) (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Primary graft patency as the endpoint, and follow-up
sec.p: The endpoint of this study was loss of primary patency due to graft stenosis. Graft failure within 30 days after surgery was counted as loss of patency only when vein quality was clearly implicated; conversely, graft failure attributable to technical error that was appropriately repaired with restoration of patency was counted as maintained patency and was not treated as an endpoint. Follow-up was performed using duplex ultrasonography every 3 months until 2 years after surgery, and every 6 months thereafter until 5 years after surgery. Graft stenosis occurring more than 1 month after surgery, or intervention for graft occlusion, was considered a loss of patency. Lesions demonstrating a peak systolic velocity of 300 cm/s within the graft, including at the proximal and distal anastomoses, on duplex ultrasonography were considered highly likely to progress to occlusion if left untreated, and were therefore treated as loss of patency irrespective of whether intervention was performed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Differences in the means of continuous variables between 2 groups were tested with the t-test using the standard error (SE); the Mann–Whitney U test was applied when equal variance could not be assumed. Analysis of variance was used when differences among 3 or more means were examined. Categorical data were compared between 2 groups with the chi-square test. Survival curves were calculated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and differences between 2 groups were tested with the log-rank test. A Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify factors influencing primary graft patency. Univariate analysis was performed for each factor, and factors with P <0.20 were entered into multivariate analysis. P <0.05 was considered significant. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to calculate cutoff values for factors associated with endpoint occurrence, and diagnostic accuracy was derived from the area under the curve (AUC). Analyses were performed using SPSS version 30 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA).

sec.title: Limb background and graft patency
sec.p: The mean age of the study population was 70.0 ± 9.7 years, and 67 patients (75.3%) were men. Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus in 70 patients (78.7%), dialysis dependence in 51 (57.3%), ischemic heart disease in 52 (58.4%), and cerebrovascular disease in 27 (30.3%). Thirty-five patients (39.3%) could not walk at the time of admission. With regard to limb severity, the W grade was mild in 30 limbs (33.7%) and severe in 59 limbs (66.3%); the I grade was 2 or 3 in 97% of limbs (grade 1 in 3 limbs, grade 2 in 4 limbs, and grade 3 in 82 limbs); and the fI grade was mild in 54 limbs (60.7%) and severe in 35 limbs (39.3%). The proximal anastomosis was constructed to the femoral artery in 45 limbs (50.6%; common femoral artery in 30, deep femoral artery in 4, and superficial femoral artery in 11 limbs). The distal anastomosis was constructed to the below-knee popliteal artery in 7 limbs (7.9%), to a crural artery in 25 limbs (28.1%; anterior tibial artery in 6, peroneal artery in 3, and posterior tibial artery in 16 limbs), and to a pedal artery in 56 limbs (62.9%; dorsalis pedis artery in 49 and plantar artery in 7 limbs). One limb underwent femorofemoral crossover bypass. A single vein graft was implanted in 82 limbs (92.1%) and a spliced vein graft in 7 limbs (7.9%). The placement technique was in situ in 60 limbs (67.4%), non-reversed in 22 limbs (24.7%), and reversed in 7 limbs (7.9%). A GSV from the crural or foot region—the territory potentially related to limb severity—was used in 55 limbs (61.8%). The GSV was judged as a poor-quality graft in 10 limbs (11.2%) (Table 1).

sec.p: The median follow-up period was 30.0 months. Primary graft patency was 72.3% at 1 year and 59.3% at 2 years (Fig. 2A). In univariate analysis, vein graft quality and W grade were significantly associated with primary graft patency (Fig. 2B, 2C). There was no significant difference in primary graft patency among I grades (P = 0.16), and no significant difference was observed for the fI grade either (57.4% in mild cases vs. 62.3% in severe cases, P = 0.56). Multivariate analysis identified poor-quality graft, severe W grade, and a history of cerebrovascular disease as independent factors related to primary graft patency (Table 2). When the 10 limbs with a poor-quality graft were excluded from the analysis (7 of which belonged to the severe W grade group), limbs with a severe W grade showed a trend toward lower primary graft patency than those with a mild W grade (P = 0.08; Fig. 2D).

sec.title: Factors related to graft patency and preplacement GSV wall thickness
sec.p: In the residual preplacement GSV segments, the mean intimal thickness was 46.6 ± 5.8 μm, the mean medial thickness was 292.0 ± 15.2 μm, and the mean intima/media (I/M) ratio was 0.17 ± 0.02. No association was found between intimal thickness and comorbid disease, whereas medial thickness was associated with ischemic heart disease and with an inability to walk at admission (Table 3). The media was significantly thinner in patients with ischemic heart disease than in those without (266 ± 16.3 μm vs. 329 ± 27.6 μm, P = 0.04), and it was likewise significantly thinner in nonambulatory patients than in ambulatory patients (254 ± 21.1 μm vs. 317 ± 20.4 μm, P = 0.04). No significant association was found between the I/M ratio and comorbid conditions. Cerebrovascular disease, identified as an independent factor for graft patency, did not affect intimal or medial thickness; nevertheless, these findings suggest that patient background may influence GSV medial thickness.

sec.p: With regard to limb severity, cases with a severe W grade showed significantly greater intimal and medial thickness than did cases with a mild W grade. In contrast, severe fI cases, which indicate deep infection, showed no significant difference in either medial or intimal thickness compared with mild cases. Comparison between I grades 2 and 3 also revealed no significant difference in intimal thickness (P = 0.40) or medial thickness (P = 0.98). From the comprehensive standpoint of the WIfI stage, severe cases tended to show greater intimal and medial thickness, but the difference did not reach significance (P = 0.06). Three GSV pathological specimens representing different degrees of limb severity are shown in Fig. 3. The intimal thickness of poor-quality grafts, which was significantly associated with primary graft patency, was 72.3 ± 33.6 μm, compared with 43.4 ± 5.0 μm for good-quality grafts, but the difference was not significant (P = 0.42). No difference in medial thickness according to vein quality was observed either (P = 0.88) (Table 4).

sec.title: Relationship between preplacement GSV wall thickness and primary graft patency
sec.p: Preplacement GSV wall thickness was compared between the 31 cases with loss of primary graft patency and the 58 cases with maintained patency. Intimal thickness was 44.1 ± 5.1 μm in the maintained group and 51.2 ± 13.7 μm in the loss group, with no significant difference (P = 0.57). In contrast, medial thickness was 349.9 ± 29.8 μm in the loss group and 261.1 ± 15.8 μm in the maintained group, demonstrating significant preoperative thickening in the loss group (P <0.01). The I/M ratio was 0.18 ± 0.02 in the loss group and 0.14 ± 0.03 in the maintained group, with no significant difference (P = 0.32). The AUC of the ROC curve for primary graft patency and medial thickness was 0.65 (95% confidence interval 0.56–0.77) (Fig. 4A). When the cutoff value for medial thickness was set at 280 μm, primary graft patency was 75.7% in cases with a medial thickness <280 μm and 43.0% in cases with a medial thickness >280 μm, representing a significant difference (P = 0.03, Fig. 4B). These findings suggest that the significant association of a severe W grade with primary graft patency is underpinned by preplacement medial thickening of the GSV and that this measurement may be useful as a preoperative predictor of primary graft patency.

caption.title: Receiver operating characteristic curve of preplacement great saphenous vein medial thickness for endpoint occurrence (A), and primary graft patency rates according to the presence or absence of medial thickening, using 280 μm as the cutoff value (B).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this cohort, poor-quality graft and severe W grade were independent factors for loss of primary graft patency that relate directly to the preplacement vein. To clarify why these factors are associated with vein graft failure after implantation, we evaluated preplacement GSV pathological specimens morphologically and examined the underlying causes. As a morphological effect of limb severity on the GSV, cases with a severe W grade showed significantly greater intimal and medial thickness than mild cases; in contrast, poor-quality grafts, which are likewise a factor in loss of primary graft patency, showed no difference in preplacement GSV intimal or medial thickness compared with good-quality veins. It can therefore be inferred that, although both factors are involved in the occurrence of loss of primary patency, the process of graft failure in which each participates differs. Past evidence has clearly demonstrated the inferior patency of poor-quality veins,4,5) and it is necessary to consider the process by which the wall thickening seen in severe W grade cases leads to graft failure.

Two healing processes are broadly involved in the development of vein graft stenosis. The first is graft remodeling, which occurs in the early period after implantation. Vein graft remodeling depends not only on the preoperative quality of the vein graft but also, to a large extent, on how a vein originally situated in a venous environment adapts and remodels when exposed to an arterial environment. In a normal adaptive response, the luminal diameter of the vein graft increases by 20%–25% relative to its preimplantation value, intimal hyperplasia is minimal, and graft wall thickness increases. This can be understood as an adaptive response in which wall thickening occurs outwardly so as to withstand arterial pressure while the lumen is preserved (the overall vessel diameter increases by approximately 35%–45% relative to the time of implantation: positive remodeling). In stenotic graft segments, by contrast, wall thickening occurs toward the luminal side, making maintenance of the lumen difficult; the principal sites of this wall thickening are the intima and the media (the overall vessel diameter shrinks relative to the preimplantation value: negative remodeling).8) This arterialization of the vein occurs dramatically within 1 month after implantation, with the vein progressively approximating an artery.9) The second process is progressive intimal hyperplasia. Intimal lesions contain mesenchymal cells with abundant extracellular matrix (ECM); after implantation, medial cell numbers decrease rapidly through cell death, and subsequent cell migration, proliferation, and ECM deposition are considered to produce intimal and medial thickening.10) As in atherosclerosis, the inflammatory response is recognized as an important contributor to graft failure. The causes of autologous vein graft failure are complex and diverse, but inflammation arising within the graft is 1 cause of loss of primary patency and is also considered a cause of progressive intimal hyperplasia.8,11) It has already been reported that activation of the inflammatory and prothrombotic pathways—which are closely interrelated—impairs the normal healing process of the graft and is consequently a major factor leading to graft stenosis or occlusion.12) From the standpoint of graft and inflammation, this is also consistent with the report that primary vein graft patency is low in patient groups with reduced levels of serum natural IgM antibody, which restrains excessively activated immune responses.13)

As Fig. 2 shows, when the timing of loss of primary patency in poor-quality grafts is considered, patency falls to approximately 50% within 3 months after surgery, which is highly likely to be related to negative remodeling, the first of the mechanisms discussed above. For the W grade, in contrast, patency at 1 month after surgery was 96% in mild cases and 95% in severe cases, and at 3 months it was 93% and 85%, respectively, a course that clearly differs from that of the poor-quality grafts described above. Poor-quality veins accounted for 10% and 12% of the mild and severe W grade groups, respectively (P = 0.79), so the risk of negative remodeling was comparable between the 2 groups. Although intimal thickness and medial thickness each differed significantly between these 2 groups, no major difference was observed in the timing of remodeling in the early period after implantation. Loss of patency occurred during the interval between 3 and 6 months after surgery, once remodeling had settled (Fig. 2C), and this trend is easier to appreciate when poor-quality grafts are excluded from the analysis (Fig. 2D). Thus, the W grade appears highly likely to be associated with graft failure mediated by intimal hyperplasia; in particular, graft surveillance was shown to be of the utmost importance for maintaining patency in the group of patients with both a severe W grade and a poor-quality graft.

Few studies have examined how limb severity affects the GSV pathophysiologically. An ex vivo study that examined the effects on the function of the cells constituting the GSV wall showed that W, I, and fI all reduce the normal function of GSV wall constituent cells.14) In that study, the fI grade contributed neither to primary graft patency nor to wall thickening. fI is unlikely to be the initial manifestation of CLTI and commonly develops after a foot wound has appeared. Compared with W, fI is in many cases transient and reversible, and when infected gangrene develops, prompt drainage is performed. The period during which the GSV is exposed to inflammation caused by fI is expected to be short relative to the duration of the accompanying foot wound, and we presume that this is why fI did not influence primary graft patency or wall thickness. In the process of intimal hyperplasia, an imbalance between the promotion and suppression of inflammation that was not present in the preplacement media is also thought to promote thickening. Because medial thickening (>280 μm) was shown here to be a factor capable of predicting loss of primary patency, it is conceivable that inflammation and ECM secretion are already promoted in the media of cases with a severe W grade.15) In addition, ECM secretion in the media is known to be significantly promoted under low-flow conditions during the process of intimal hyperplasia,10) and because distal bypass accounts for the majority of the present cohort, in which vein graft flow is limited, the pathophysiological relationship between preoperative medial thickening and postimplantation changes in the wall is an issue that should be verified. As discussed above, the mechanisms of reduced patency appear to differ between poor-quality grafts, which are accompanied by negative remodeling within 3 months after surgery, and cases with a severe W grade, in which slowly progressive intimal hyperplasia develops beyond 3 months after surgery. On the basis of the results of the present study, we postulate the following sequence for the effect of the W grade on graft wall thickening. First, in cases with a severe W grade, promotion of inflammation and enhanced ECM secretion in the media are already present at the time of implantation, and medial thickening is confirmed. When a vein in this state is exposed to the arterial environment after implantation, the responses of remodeling and intimal hyperplasia are more pronounced than in mild cases, and as a result, the risk of progressive intimal hyperplasia increases. Furthermore, considering that approximately 10% of cases contain a poor-quality graft irrespective of the W grade, this reactive process may become even more marked. The influence of limb severity on the GSV wall is thus a phenomenon that deserves full consideration, and its elucidation may become a key to overcoming graft failure in the future.

This study has the following limitations. First, it was a single-center study, and because it was restricted to cases with a GSV pathological specimen, the analysis was limited to only 89 cases. Second, although the GSV was harvested from the affected limb and used for reconstruction in all cases, it was harvested from the thigh in 35 cases (39.3%), so the extent to which limb severity exerts an influence is open to question. Third, the GSV was not fixed in a uniformly distended state under intraluminal pressure in every case; therefore, wall thickness measurements were not performed under identical conditions in all cases.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Limb severity is a significant adverse factor for the primary patency of vein grafts; in cases with a severe W grade in particular, significantly greater preplacement wall thickness of the GSV was observed than in mild cases. Medial thickening of the preplacement GSV is considered to be a factor involved in graft patency and to contribute to the clinical significance of the W grade.

sec.title: Ethics approval and consent to participate
sec.p: This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Asahikawa Medical University (approval number 22015) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Because of the retrospective design, the requirement for written informed consent was waived; instead, the study was disclosed to the public and participants were given the opportunity to opt out.
